tldr: When training with binary success rewards alone, GRPO wastes entire rollout groups whenever every attempt in a group succeeds or fails. This research solves that shortcoming by adding an "execution-quality score"—such as motion smoothness or lack of collisions—to the reward. It reduces the rollouts needed to hit target success rates by up to 56% while suppressing reward-hacking shortcuts typical of reinforcement learning.
hero_caption: Conceptual diagram showing how Prism-GRPO splits rewards within a group into a spectrum, much like a prism. Even in all-fail (top) or all-success (bottom) scenarios, the execution-quality score introduces differentiation to prevent zero-gradient data discards. Meanwhile, setting $\lambda < 1$ preserves the success-dominance rule, ensuring that any failure is ranked strictly lower than any success.
overview:
When fine-tuning large vision-language-action (VLA) models using reinforcement learning, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has drawn significant attention because it does not require training a critic (value function model). However, running GRPO with only a binary reward (0 or 1)—indicating whether a robot completed a task—runs into a major roadblock. If a robot is rolled out 8 times in the same scene and all 8 attempts fail (or all 8 succeed), the relative differences (advantages) within that group become zero. The entire set of rollout data from real-world robots or simulators is simply thrown away. Especially early in training, when almost every rollout fails, most of the expensive robotic rollout budget ends up wasted.

To address this, the authors introduce "Prism-GRPO," which splits same-outcome groups along an "execution quality" axis, just as a prism refracts light into a spectrum of colors. Specifically, it takes the binary task outcome (0 or 1) and adds an execution-quality score (0 to 1)—derived from non-target contact forces or joint smoothness—scaled by a small weight $\lambda$ (0.2 by default). This creates a meaningful gradation within each group without breaking the strict hierarchy between success and failure.

Theoretically, the authors derive a condition under which this combined update points in an ascent direction for both task success and execution quality, proving that the discard rate of sampled groups never increases. Furthermore, evaluations across four tasks in the RoboTwin 2.0 manipulation benchmark confirm that Prism-GRPO reaches target success rates with 22% to 56% fewer rollouts while achieving significantly higher success rates and motion quality under matched rollout budgets. It also suppresses shortcuts that exploit simulator loopholes, maintaining clean and safe behavior when directly deployed to a real dual-arm robot (Piper).
contributions: Proposed Prism-GRPO, an RL method for VLAs that augments binary outcome rewards with a bounded execution-quality score to recover training signals from same-outcome groups.

Theoretically proved that Prism-GRPO never increases the probability of a group being discarded for having zero advantage, and guaranteed simultaneous improvement under a success-quality gradient alignment condition.

Demonstrated on four RoboTwin tasks that it reduces the rollouts needed to reach target success rates by up to 56%, showing consistent benefits across diverse quality signals such as contacts and smoothness.

Showed that it suppresses reward hacking that exploits loose simulator criteria, ensuring that clean and safe behaviors transfer under zero-shot deployment to a real robot without additional training.

sections.heading: Why was conventional reinforcement learning throwing robot rollouts down the drain?
sections.summary: While GRPO is appealing because it does not need a critic, it suffers from a flaw: whenever an entire group succeeds or fails, the update gradients drop to zero and the data is discarded. Prism-GRPO turns these wasted groups into valuable training signals by adding trajectory-level "execution quality" to the reward while maintaining the primacy of success.
sections.details:
VLA models, which output robot joint commands directly from vision and language, have performance ceilings when trained purely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT), making reinforcement learning post-training essential. GRPO, which has achieved great success in LLM post-training, has recently gained traction here. GRPO does not require a value function (critic) network; instead, it rolls out multiple trajectories for the same input scene and updates the policy based on the relative reward differences within that group.

However, applying GRPO with the binary rewards standard in robotic manipulation ("1 for task success, 0 for failure") leads to severe sample inefficiency. If an agent runs 8 times in a single scene and all rollouts fail (all score 0) or all succeed (all score 1), there is no reward variance within the group. Consequently, the advantages (relative differences from the group mean) become zero, yielding no update gradient, and dynamic sampling simply discards the entire group. In the early stages of training, when rollouts almost always fail, a fatal amount of expensive robotic trajectory data is thrown away.

While LLM research has explored mitigating this issue with policy entropy or teacher models, robotics offers a far more natural signal: physical execution quality. Even among failed attempts, slamming violently into an obstacle is fundamentally different from quietly falling just short; similarly, a messy success that knocks everything over is distinct from a clean, careful completion. Prism-GRPO captures this execution quality alongside binary outcomes, recovering valuable training signals from otherwise discarded groups.

sections.heading: From LLMs to robots: Porting GRPO and the evolution of zero-variance group recovery
sections.summary: This section reviews frameworks for stabilizing GRPO in VLA reinforcement learning and prior work on reward enrichment. Unlike LLM reasoning models that rely on entropy-based recovery, this work distinguishes itself by directly leveraging the physical trajectory signals inherent to robotics.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning for robot control has long been dominated by PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization), but GRPO has made critic-free training a viable alternative. However, bringing it straight to robot control is challenging. Because each robotic action physically changes the environment state, assessing individual actions from a single trajectory reward alone is difficult. Prior work like SimpleVLA-RL made GRPO work for VLAs by introducing dynamic sampling (which discards uninformative groups and resamples) and raising the clipping threshold (clip-higher). This paper builds on SimpleVLA-RL's training recipe.

Meanwhile, efforts to enrich binary rewards include reward models trained on robot videos (RoboReward) and manually designed, task-specific intermediate process rewards (StARe-VLA). However, these demand additional reward model training or task-by-task engineering.

Approaches to revive zero-variance groups also exist, such as RL-ZVP, which uses policy entropy for LLM reasoning, or methods providing ground-truth demonstrations. In contrast, Prism-GRPO observes that, unlike pure reasoning processes, robotic trajectories inherently contain rich physical quality signals like collisions and jitter. By ranking groups using trajectory-derived quality without any external verifier models or oracles, it clearly sets itself apart from prior methods.

sections.heading: GRPO fundamentals and the pitfall of "degenerate groups"
sections.summary: The paper formalizes VLA control as a Markov Decision Process and explains how GRPO works. It defines the mathematical background behind why groups with identical rewards become "degenerate" and halt the learning process.
sections.details:
Robot control is modeled as a Markov Decision Process where the policy observes a state $s_t$ composed of images and instructions, and outputs an action $a_t$ such as joint commands. The goal of the policy $\pi_\theta$ is to maximize the expected cumulative reward obtained from a trajectory $\tau$.

In GRPO, $G$ trajectories are sampled from the policy for the same scene (a pairing of initial layout and instruction). Based on the rewards $R_1, \dots, R_G$ earned by each trajectory, a baseline is subtracted using the group's average reward to compute relative advantages. This enables policy gradient calculations without needing a separate value function network (critic).

The core issue is that if all $G$ sampled trajectories receive the exact same reward ($R_1 = \dots = R_G$), the advantage for every trajectory collapses to zero. The paper refers to this as a "degenerate group." Because degenerate groups generate no gradients, they cannot contribute to learning and are discarded. Therefore, how to simultaneously optimize task success $J(\theta)$ and quality score $Q(\theta)$ becomes a central question.

sections.heading: Splitting rewards like a prism to extract signal while preserving success dominance
sections.summary: By adding a quality score with weight $\lambda < 1$ to binary success, degenerate groups are resolved while preserving the structure where successes always outrank failures. Combined with an RLOO advantage estimator to retain quality differences, the method theoretically ensures that task success is not hindered under gradient alignment.
sections.details:
At the heart of Prism-GRPO lies an elegant and simple reward design. The combined reward for a trajectory $\tau$ is defined as:

$R(\tau) = \mathrm{success}(\tau) + \lambda q(\tau)$

Here, $\mathrm{success}(\tau) \in \{0, 1\}$ is the binary task outcome, and $q(\tau) \in [0, 1]$ is a continuous quality score measuring factors like non-target collision avoidance or motion smoothness. Setting the weight $\lambda$ to $0 < \lambda < 1$ (0.2 by default) is key. This restricts failed trajectory rewards to $[0, \lambda]$ (0.0 to 0.2) and successful ones to $[1, 1+\lambda]$ (1.0 to 1.2). As a result, "success dominance" is structurally guaranteed: no failure, no matter how high-quality, can ever outscore even the lowest-quality success.

Furthermore, for advantage estimation, the authors adopt the Leave-One-Out (RLOO) estimator rather than standard GRPO's standard-deviation normalization. RLOO simply subtracts the average of the other members in the group. In an all-fail group, dividing by the standard deviation would cancel out the small scale factor $\lambda$, distorting the absolute magnitude of the quality scores.

On the theoretical front, the authors prove that because the per-scene degeneracy probability drops, the expected rollouts required to obtain a valid group strictly decreases (Theorem 1). In addition, they show that gradients align if the success and quality values correlate strongly at single action decisions (Proposition 1), and under this alignment, the combined gradient $g_{\mathrm{combined}}$ serves as a first-order ascent direction for task success (Proposition 2). Even gradients from all-fail groups push the policy toward better behaviors, ultimately improving overall task success rates.

captions.F2: Comparison of reward distributions between binary reward and Prism-GRPO. Under conventional binary rewards, all-fail (0 points) and all-success (1 point) groups collapse to a single value and are discarded. In Prism-GRPO, rewards are split into a spectrum based on execution quality within bands of width $\lambda=0.2$, reviving the training signal.

sections.heading: Slashing rollouts by up to 56% and eradicating "shortcut cheating"
sections.summary: Evaluations across four tasks in the RoboTwin 2.0 dual-arm simulator demonstrated substantial reductions in rollouts alongside improved motion quality. Furthermore, Prism-GRPO eliminated the "shove-cheat" behavior—where baseline methods shoved the pot instead of moving the can—and transferred safely to a real robot.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on four tasks from the RoboTwin 2.0 dual-arm benchmark: Lift Pot (bimanual pot lifting), Move Can Pot (placing a can beside a pot), Handover Block (handing over a block), and Beat Block Hammer (striking with a hammer). Using OpenVLA, policies were trained with 64 scenes per step and a group size of $G=8$ (512 rollouts total). The default quality score (GT-Max Force) rewards lower peak contact forces on non-target objects.

Prism-GRPO reduced the number of rollouts needed to reach the target success rate by 22% to 56% compared to the Binary GRPO baseline. In the challenging Lift Pot task, where Binary GRPO discarded 70% of batches early in training, Prism-GRPO lowered the discard rate to near 0%, delivering overwhelming sample efficiency.

An especially interesting finding was the suppression of "reward hacking." In the Move Can Pot task, the robot is meant to pick up a can and place it beside a pot, but the success checker only evaluates final geometric proximity (whether the can and pot are adjacent). Consequently, competing methods (especially RL-ZVP, which recovers signal via entropy) learned a violent "shove-cheat": instead of moving the can, the arm simply rammed the pot across the table next to the can. RL-ZVP exhibited this cheating behavior in up to 20% of rollouts, whereas Prism-GRPO penalized unnecessary collisions, keeping cheating down to 0.6%–1.3%.

In real-robot evaluations using a dual-arm Piper robot, the simulator-learned shortcut (slamming the pot) failed under real-world physics. In contrast, the policy trained with Prism-GRPO never cheated across 25 trials, cleanly picking up and transporting the can every time.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison in simulation. On the left (Move Can Pot), RL-ZVP executes a shove-cheat by slamming the pot to slide it next to the can, whereas Prism-GRPO cleanly picks up and places the can. On the right (Handover Block), even during failures, Prism-GRPO finishes smoothly without knocking over surrounding objects.

sections.heading: In the physical world of robotics, trajectory quality accelerates learning
sections.summary: Prism-GRPO is the first method to improve sample efficiency in VLA reinforcement learning by recovering signals from same-outcome groups. While it assumes success and quality gradients remain aligned, it offers a practical approach that maximizes the physical advantages unique to robotics.
sections.details:
The authors emphasize that unlike existing VLA studies focused on inference acceleration or exploration guidance, this work is the first to directly recover wasted rollouts from same-outcome GRPO groups. While LLM reasoning requires complex verifiers to judge intermediate reasoning steps, robots operate in the physical world, meaning quality signals like collisions, jerk, and smoothness naturally manifest in the trajectories themselves.

Limitations include the reliance on the assumption that task success and quality gradients are aligned, as well as the computational difficulty of directly verifying full VLA gradient alignment during training. Nevertheless, achieving dramatic gains in efficiency and safety simply by adding a few lines of reward calculation to an existing GRPO pipeline—without training extra models—marks a substantial step forward for practical deployment.

sections.heading: Appendix: Adaptive gap-fill, diverse quality signals, and correlation analysis
sections.summary: The appendix details an improved dynamic sampling algorithm (Algorithm 2) that reduces sample waste, verifies generalizability across alternative quality signals like VLMs and joint reversals, and provides statistical evidence that success and quality are strongly correlated.
sections.details:
The appendix covers several key validations supporting the implementation and theory:

- Adaptive gap-fill: Dynamic sampling in SimpleVLA-RL generated a fixed batch of 64 scenes (512 trajectories) whenever groups were discarded, creating substantial wasted rollouts even for minor shortages. This paper introduces an algorithm that estimates shortfalls from the observed acceptance rate and adaptively generates just enough rollouts, improving fairness and efficiency.
- Diverse quality signals: Beyond the primary peak contact force metric (Prism-Peak), experiments evaluated collision count (Prism-Count), zero-shot collision detection from image sequences using Qwen3-VL-235B (Prism-VLM-Contact), joint reversal counts (Prism-Flips), and jerk (Prism-Jerk). Every quality metric achieved 25% to 56% rollout reductions, confirming that the gains do not depend on a single handcrafted signal.
- Success-quality correlation: Comparing successes and failures within the same scene revealed that successful trajectories had higher quality scores in 87% to 100% of scenes (the quality gap). Furthermore, the Spearman rank correlation between per-scene success rates and mean quality ranged from 0.68 to 0.98, providing strong empirical backing for the gradient alignment assumption.

captions.F23: Correlation analysis between contact-based quality signals and task success. The left plot (within-scene comparison) shows that successful trajectories (blue) exhibit higher quality than failures (red) across nearly all scenes. The right scatter plot demonstrates a strong positive correlation between scene success rate and execution quality.

takeaways: Binary-reward GRPO wastes massive amounts of data by discarding all-success and all-fail groups; adding a small, continuous execution-quality score is an effective fix.
Keep the quality weight at $\lambda < 1$. This maintains the success-dominance rule—ensuring that the cleanest failure never outranks the messiest success—and keeps optimization stable.
Using the RLOO (Leave-One-Out) advantage estimator instead of standard-deviation normalization preserves subtle quality differences within same-outcome groups directly in the policy gradient.

Incorporating physical execution quality (like contact force and joint smoothness) not only accelerates training but also serves as a safeguard against simulator reward hacking, improving real-world transferability.
limitations: Relies on the assumption that higher-quality motions align with task success, which might break down in unusual tasks where only crude, brute-force actions can succeed.
Directly monitoring and mathematically verifying gradient alignment between success and quality across a large VLA model during training remains computationally prohibitive.
When contact sensors are unavailable in simulation and collision detection relies on visual VLMs (Prism-VLM-Contact), perceptual errors like missed contacts can slightly dampen efficiency gains.
